segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but it was so that the works of God might be revealed in him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: We must do the works of the one who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he spat on the ground and made mud with the saliva, and he smeared the mud on the man’s eyes,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: (which means “Sent”). So he went and washed, and came back seeing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the neighbors and those who used to see him before as a beggar said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Isn’t this the man who used to sit and beg?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This is the man.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Others were saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “No, but he looks like him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He himself kept saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I am the one.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How then were your eyes opened?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The man called Jesus made mud and smeared it on my eyes and said to me, ‘Go to Siloam and wash.’ So I went and washed, and I gained my sight.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where is he?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I don’t know.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought the man who had once been blind to the Pharisees.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now it was a Sabbath on the day Jesus made the mud and opened his eyes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Pharisees also asked him again how he had gained his sight. He said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So some of the Pharisees said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Others said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can a man who is a sinner perform such signs?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there was a division among them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to the blind man again,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What do you say about him, since it was your eyes he opened?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is a prophet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jewish leaders did not believe that he had been blind and had gained his sight until they summoned the parents of the man who had gained his sight

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and asked them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is this your son, who you say was born blind? How then does he now see?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His parents answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We know that this is our son and that he was born blind.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: But how he now sees we do not know, nor do we know who opened his eyes. Ask him; he is of age. He will speak for himself.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His parents said this because they were afraid of the Jewish leaders, for the Jewish leaders had already agreed that if anyone acknowledged him as the Messiah, that person would be put out of the synagogue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why his parents said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He is of age; ask him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So for a second time they summoned the man who had been blind and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I know: I was blind, and now I see.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I told you already, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? You don’t want to become his disciples too, do you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They hurled abuse at him and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are that man’s disciple, but we are disciples of Moses.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We know that God has spoken to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The man answered them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Now here is the amazing thing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: We know that God does not listen to sinners, but if anyone is devout and does his will, God listens to that person.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Since time began it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a person born blind.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You were born entirely in sins, and you are teaching us?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they threw him out.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, and when he found him he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you believe in the Son of Man?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “And who is he, sir, so that I may believe in him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I believe, Lord,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he worshiped him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Some of the Pharisees who were with him heard this and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Surely we are not blind too?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If you were blind, you would have no sin. But now you say, ‘We see.’ Your sin remains.”

notes.traditional: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him
notes.note: The Greek has only “but so that,” with no verb, and most translations supply something like “this happened” or “it was.” A minority of interpreters punctuate differently, ending the sentence after “sinned” and attaching the clause to verse 4: “But so that the works of God may be revealed in him, we must do the works…” That reading avoids implying that the man was made blind for this purpose; the traditional punctuation is followed here as the majority view.

notes.phrase: We must do the works of the one who sent me
notes.traditional: I must work the works of him that sent me
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read “we must,” which draws the disciples into Jesus’s work; many later manuscripts read “I must,” the reading behind the King James Version. A few early witnesses also read “the one who sent us.” Most modern editions and translations adopt “we … sent me,” as here.

Siloam was a pool at the southern end of Jerusalem, fed by a water channel from the Gihon spring. Its Hebrew name, Shiloah, resembles the Hebrew verb “to send,” and John’s gloss invites the reader to connect the pool with Jesus, who repeatedly describes himself in this Gospel as the one sent by the Father (as in verse 4).

The detail explains the Pharisees’ objection in verse 16. Kneading appears among the kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath in later rabbinic lists, and healing a chronic, non-life-threatening condition on the Sabbath was widely considered impermissible. Making mud and healing a man blind from birth would have been seen as a breach on both counts.

The Greek says simply “the Jews,” but everyone in this scene is Jewish, including the man, his parents and Jesus. The group meant is the authorities who conduct the inquiry (the Pharisees of verses 13–16) and who have power to expel people from the synagogue (verse 22). Scholars are divided over how best to render the term in John; this translation uses “the Jewish leaders” where the narrower group is clearly in view.

The Greek word is the one traditionally rendered “Christ.” Here it is not a name but a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and the question is whether Jesus is that figure. “Messiah” conveys this to a modern reader, and several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

The Greek is a single adjective found only in John’s Gospel (here and at 12:42 and 16:2). It means exclusion from the local Jewish community’s gathering, which carried heavy social as well as religious consequences. Scholars debate how formal such expulsion was in Jesus’s lifetime, and many think the wording also reflects the experience of John’s first readers later in the century.

This is not an invitation to praise God for the healing but a solemn formula calling on someone to tell the truth or confess, as when Joshua says the same to Achan in Joshua 7:19. The authorities are putting the man on oath and pressing him to agree with their verdict on Jesus.
The Greek idiom is literally “from the age,” using a time-word, not the word for “world.” It means from the remote past or from the very beginning, and is rendered accordingly.

The earliest and best manuscripts read “Son of Man”; many later manuscripts read “Son of God,” which is the reading of the King James Version. “Son of God” is generally regarded as a later change toward the more familiar confession, and modern editions read “Son of Man.”

The same Greek form of address appears in verse 36 and verse 38. It ranges from a polite “sir” to “Lord” as a confession. In verse 36 the man does not yet know who the Son of Man is, so “sir” fits; in verse 38 it accompanies belief and worship, so “Lord” is used. The Greek leaves the shift to the reader, and some translations use “Lord” in both verses.

Occurs three times in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2) and should be rendered identically each time so readers can connect the passages.
A key Johannine term that some versions render “miracle” or “miraculous sign”; it needs one rendering across the Gospels, Acts and Revelation.
The vocative addressed to Jesus ranges from polite “sir” to confessional “Lord,” and a consistent policy for choosing between them is needed across the Gospels.
Usually “regain sight” in healing stories but also “look up”; for a man born blind “regain” is wrong, so the healing sense needs a decision that works across the Gospels and Acts.
